title: Galactic Stellar Streams, Tidal Tails and the Magellanic System: Disruption, Orbit and Dark-Matter Substructure Budgets Against Density and Energy Bounds

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Settle in.
paragraphs: Welcome in. I am Professor Kazuo Watanabe, and this is Galactic Stellar Streams, Tidal Tails and the Magellanic System: Disruption, Orbit and Dark-Matter Substructure Budgets Against Density and Energy Bounds. This is lesson 1 of 1 in the full thirty-minute build of this class. In this lesson we take the class's own material in order — nothing here is imported, and nothing is asked later that is not taught here first. We begin here: Settle in.

Settle in. I am Professor Kazuo Watanabe, and this is Galactic Stellar Streams, Tidal Tails and the Magellanic System: Disruption, Orbit and Dark-Matter Substructure Budgets Against Density and Energy Bounds. This class is built on real papers — deposited, citable work. I will present each paper and what it reports; that presentation is the lesson. At the end I will ask you questions on what was taught here — nothing else.
Here is the next piece of the material, in the order the class presents it.

'Cold Streams as Calorimeters: A Velocity-Dispersion Bound on Dark-Matter Substructure Heating'. Its stated result: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): allowed_heating_km2_s2 = 3.000; max_heating_rate_km2_s2_per_Gyr = 1.000; encounter_rate_per_Gyr = 4.295; single_kick_km_s = 4.096; kick_heating_per_encounter_km2_s2 = 16.78; encounters_allowed = 0.1788; max_subhalo_mass_Msun = 4.229e+06; orbital_period_Gyr = 0.5649; dispersion_to_circular_ratio = 0.0092; free_streaming_scale_proxy_kpc = 6.136.
Now we go one step further into the material.

'Gaia-Enceladus Debris: A Merger Energy, Mass-Ratio and Radialisation Budget'. Its stated result: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): halo_mass_ratio = 4.000; stellar_mass_ratio_to_mw_stars = 0.1200; specific_radial_energy_km2_s2 = 31,250.0; tangential_dispersion_km_s = 55.90; radial_to_tangential_ratio = 3.162; dynamical_friction_time_Gyr = 0.1756; orbits_since_merger = 24.65; merger_kinetic_energy_erg = 6.214e+58; specific_angular_momentum_scale_kpc_km_s = 838.5; anisotropy_energy_fraction_radi
The next piece is where this starts to come together.

'NGC 5466 and Its Forty-Five Degree Tails: A Mass-Loss Budget for a Low-Concentration Cluster'. Its stated result: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): tidal_radius_pc = 71.09; orbital_period_Gyr = 0.4350; tail_length_kpc = 12.57; mass_loss_rate_Msun_per_Gyr = 5,747.6; remaining_lifetime_Gyr = 8.699; escape_velocity_km_s = 6.253; tidal_to_half_light_ratio = 6.463; orbits_completed = 27.59; cumulative_mass_lost_Msun = 1.558e+05; crossing_time_Myr = 11.95.
Listen carefully here — this piece carries weight in the questions later.

'Palomar 5 and Its Tidal Tails: A Cluster Evaporation Budget at the Edge of Dissolution'. Its stated result: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): tidal_radius_pc = 49.41; orbital_period_Gyr = 0.5144; tail_length_kpc = 8.908; mass_loss_rate_Msun_per_Gyr = 2,332.8; remaining_lifetime_Gyr = 5.144; escape_velocity_km_s = 2.272; relaxation_proxy_Gyr = 0.1973; tail_to_cluster_mass_ratio = 2.236; tidal_to_half_light_ratio = 2.470; dispersion_crossing_time_Myr = 35.56.
We take the pieces in order, because each one stands on the last.

'The ATLAS Stream: Width, Dispersion and the Mass of a Fully Dissolved Progenitor'. Its stated result: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): stream_length_kpc = 9.774; tidal_radius_implied_pc = 45.00; progenitor_mass_Msun = 4,374.0; orbital_period_Gyr = 0.7406; width_growth_time_Gyr = 0.0440; length_growth_rate_kpc_per_Gyr = 3.258; width_to_length_ratio = 0.0092; circular_velocity_km_s = 207.4; escape_scale_km_s = 0.9144; dispersion_to_escape_ratio = 2.187.
Stay with me, because the next piece builds directly on that one.

'The GD-1 Gap: An Impulse Budget for a Dark Subhalo Encounter with a Cold Stellar Stream'. Its stated result: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): impulse_kick_km_s = 2.867; gap_length_kpc = 1.466; stream_length_kpc = 9.346; width_to_length_ratio = 0.0070; kick_to_dispersion_ratio = 1.365; encounter_duration_Myr = 3.259; subhalo_mean_density_Msun_per_pc3 = 0.0884; gap_fraction_of_stream = 0.1569; dispersion_energy_km2_s2 = 4.410; max_subhalo_mass_for_kick_below_dispersion_Msun = 7.324e+06.
Here is the next piece of the material, in the order the class presents it.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Take the paper “Cold Streams as Calorimeters: A Velocity-Dispersion Bound on Dark-Matter Substructure Heating”. Its stated result is: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): allowed_heating_km2_s2 = 3.000; max_heating_rate_km2_s2_per_Gyr = 1.000; encounter_rate_per_Gyr = 4.295; single_kick_km_s = 4.096; kick_heating_per_encounter_km2_s2 = 16.78; encounters_allowed = 0.1788; max_subhalo_mass_Msun = 4.229e+06; orbital_p (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong. The worked answer: A strong answer restates the claim without borrowing the paper’s wording, then names a test the paper itself would accept — here, the natural test is to recompute or re-measure the headline quantity in the stated result and check it against the paper’s own number, under the paper’s own stated assumptions.

Let us gather what this lesson taught, in order: Settle in; 'Cold Streams as Calorimeters: A Velocity-Dispersion Bound on Dark-Matter Substructure Heating'; 'Gaia-Enceladus Debris: A Merger Energy, Mass-Ratio and Radialisation Budget'; 'NGC 5466 and Its Forty-Five Degree Tails: A Mass-Loss Budget for a Low-Concentration Cluster'; 'Palomar 5 and Its Tidal Tails: A Cluster Evaporation Budget at the Edge of Dissolution'; 'The ATLAS Stream: Width, Dispersion and the Mass of a Fully Dissolved Progenitor'. Those are the pieces — hold them in that order, because the questions follow the same road.

That is the lesson, whole. Below it are the questions — every one of them drawn from what was just taught, and nothing else. The full text of this lesson stays open beside the questions, and going back to read a piece again is learning, not cheating. When you are ready, begin.
